per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid, a person is generally eligible for **CAP/DA services** if they are a **Medicaid beneficiary** and meet both the program’s **general medical-necessity standards** and the **specific CAP/DA waiver criteria**. The key requirements are:

## General eligibility criteria for CAP/DA

A beneficiary must:

- **Be enrolled in NC Medicaid.** The policy states the person must be enrolled in the NC Medicaid program, and eligibility category restrictions can still make someone ineligible for this service. § 2.1.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current per amendment check).

- **Meet NC Medicaid’s general coverage standards.** The service must be:
  - individualized, specific, and consistent with the person’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis;
  - not more than the person needs;
  - safely furnished;
  - not replace an equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide; and
  - not provided mainly for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider. § 3.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current).

- **Meet nursing-facility level of care (LOC) requirements for HCBS.** The person must meet the required HCBS nursing facility LOC as determined by NC Medicaid and need long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, tied to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need. § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

- **Show a reasonable indication of need for CAP/DA services.** A completed CAP assessment must show a reasonable indication that the individual will need at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within 30 calendar days of the evaluation. § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

- **Have an approved, signed service plan.** The beneficiary must have a signed service plan authorizing one or more waiver services on a monthly basis to prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management. The policy also allows short-term approval for equipment, modification, or technology needed to return to or remain in the primary private residence and avoid institutional placement. § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

- **Be able to remain safely in the home or approved setting.** The beneficiary must be able to maintain health, safety, and well-being in the primary private residence or an approved location with formal and informal supports. § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

- **Have paid care needs that fit within waiver cost limits.** The person’s paid care needs must be maintainable within the average institutional cost of the CAP/DA waiver. § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

- **Have a primary physician.** The beneficiary must have a primary physician who can link and coordinate medical services. § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

- **Have an emergency backup and disaster plan.** The plan must specify who will provide care if key staff are unavailable, the primary caregiver has an emergency, or there is a public health emergency such as severe weather or a pandemic. § 3.2.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

## When CAP/DA is not covered

NC Medicaid will not cover CAP/DA if the beneficiary does **not** meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0 or the criteria in Section 3.0. § 4.1, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

## Bottom line

In plain terms, CAP/DA is for an **NC Medicaid-enrolled adult who meets nursing-facility level of care, needs waiver services to avoid institutional placement, can be served safely in the community with supports, has an approved service plan, and whose care can be maintained within program cost limits**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current).

If you want, I can also give you:
1. a **short screening checklist** for advocates, or  
2. the **differences between CAP/DA eligibility and CAP/C eligibility**.

per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid’s **Orthotics & Prosthetics** policy, the specifically not-covered items are certain **devices/equipment/supplies**, and coverage generally requires that the item meet medical-necessity, ordering, encounter, and treatment-plan criteria.

## Specifically not covered

NC Medicaid does **not** cover the following under this policy:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience** or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices** or **duplicate devices** kept at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**  
  — *Orthotics & Prosthetics* § 4.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

There are also broader general noncoverage rules. NC Medicaid will not cover the item/service if:

- the beneficiary does **not** meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does **not** meet the coverage criteria in Section 3.0;
- the item/service **duplicates another provider’s** procedure, product, or service; or
- the item/service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**  
  — *Orthotics & Prosthetics* § 4.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

For coverage, the policy says the orthotic or prosthetic must be:

- **Ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- **Medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level
- **Appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place
- Supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering physician/PA/NP related to the primary reason for the device, occurring **no more than 6 months before initiation**
- Subject to **at least annual review** of the beneficiary’s need by the ordering physician/PA/NP  
  — *Orthotics & Prosthetics* § 3.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy further requires that orthotic and prosthetic devices be:

- a **reasonable and medically necessary part** of the beneficiary’s treatment plan;
- **consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the beneficiary’s functional limitations and symptoms; and
- **of high quality**, with replacement parts available and obtainable  
  — *Orthotics & Prosthetics* § 3.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Item-specific medical necessity standards

The policy also distinguishes between orthotics and prosthetics:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**.
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary when they **replace all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary must require the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes**.  
  — *Orthotics & Prosthetics* § 3.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

A device is generally covered only if it is properly ordered, medically necessary, tied to the beneficiary’s diagnosis and treatment plan, supported by a recent face-to-face encounter, and reviewed at least annually. It is specifically not covered if it is for convenience/comfort, a backup/duplicate, for a nursing-facility resident, covered by another agency, or hospice-related equipment/supplies under this policy.  
Current authoritative source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Orthotics & Prosthetics**; I checked for amendments and the tool returned this document as current.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services, the policy sets specific **entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria** in Clinical Coverage Policy 8C. Providers also must document these criteria in the clinical record. This is the current policy effective **April 15, 2025**, and I did not find any amendment superseding it. [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets entrance criteria when all of the following are present:

- A current **DSM-5 diagnosis** (or subsequent edition).
- The beneficiary presents **behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment** consistent with and associated with the current diagnosis.
- If a **higher level of care** is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary is refusing that service, outpatient services may be provided until the higher level is available or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care.
- The beneficiary is **capable of developing skills** to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions.
- There is **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective**, based on North Carolina community practice standards. [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.1

## Continued service criteria
To continue services, the beneficiary must meet:

### 1. At least one of these:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary continues to be **at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- There is a **tenuous nature of the functional gains**.

### 2. And at least one additional criterion:
- The beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, but **additional goals are indicated** as shown by documented symptoms; or
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress** toward meeting goals, and there is documentation supporting that. [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.2

## Discharge criteria
Discharge is appropriate when any of the following applies:

- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the treatment plan goals;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wishes to receive services**; or
- The beneficiary, based on presentation and lack of improvement despite modifications to the treatment plan, **requires a more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards. [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3

## Documentation requirement
The provider’s record must include **documentation of entrance criteria, continued service criteria, and discharge criteria** as part of the clinical documentation requirements. [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 7.3.1

If you want, I can also pull these into a **short advocate-friendly checklist** for denials, audits, or medical-record review.

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries under 21, the EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition. But EPSDT does **not** waive prior approval requirements, and the therapy still must be properly ordered. Under Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, orders may come from an MD, DO, DPM, CNM, PA, or NP, and a verbal or written order must be obtained before services begin. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Effect of EPSDT on outpatient therapy coverage

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A includes an “EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age.” That provision ties coverage to the federal EPSDT standard in 42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r). The retrieved text also shows limits on that exception: EPSDT does not require coverage for services that are “unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational,” or “not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.” [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

For outpatient specialized therapies specifically, the pediatric sections show that beneficiaries under 21 are evaluated under child-specific medical-necessity standards. For example:

- speech-language therapy includes criteria specifically applicable to Medicaid beneficiaries under 21; and
- medical-necessity visit guidelines for beneficiaries under 21 set pediatric visit ranges and authorization periods for speech-language and audiology therapy. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

Just as important, the policy expressly states that if a service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, being under age 21 “does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.” So EPSDT may support coverage beyond ordinary limitations, but it does not remove utilization-control requirements built into the policy. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A’s ordering-practitioner section lists the practitioners who may order services:

- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP) [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

For treatment services, the policy further requires:

- a verbal or written order before the start of services;
- verbal orders must be documented in the beneficiary’s health record and countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days;
- verbal orders are valid up to six months from the documented date received;
- written orders are valid up to six months from the date of the physician’s signature; and
- backdating is not allowed. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Bottom line

For a Medicaid beneficiary under 21, EPSDT can support coverage of medically necessary outpatient therapy even when standard policy limits might otherwise be restrictive, so long as the service is medical in nature and not unsafe, ineffective, or experimental. But the child’s age does **not** remove prior approval requirements, and therapy must still be ordered by an authorized practitioner under Policy 10A.  

I checked amendments for Policy 10A, and the current authoritative document remains **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, effective February 1, 2025**.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services for some beneficiaries who live in assisted-living-type settings, but only if they meet the congregate-setting PCS criteria.

Under the congregate-settings PCS policy, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who resides in a North Carolina licensed Adult Care Home or combination home, or in certain licensed group homes, and who also meets the functional and medical-necessity criteria. The policy requires, among other things, unmet need for qualifying ADLs and residence in a licensed congregate facility. It also requires an eligibility assessment conducted in the beneficiary’s congregate facility. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), §§ 3.2.1, 5.4.3.

It is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet the Section 3.0 coverage criteria, and additional non-covered rules apply if, for example, the service is provided somewhere other than the beneficiary’s primary congregate living setting, exceeds the approved amount, or required assessment/reassessment rules are not met. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), §§ 4.1, 4.2.1.

So the short answer is:

- **Yes, potentially covered** in an assisted living facility **if** the facility fits the policy’s licensed congregate-setting categories and the beneficiary meets the PCS eligibility criteria.
- **No, not automatically** just because the person lives in assisted living.

For comparison, the separate in-home PCS policy applies to services in a beneficiary’s **private residence**, not congregate facilities. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3l-state-plan-personal-care-services-pcs/download?attachment), effective Jan. 1, 2026.

- the ADL thresholds for approval, or

per_question.question: What is the treatment plan (plan of care) requirement for outpatient therapy services under NC Medicaid policy 10A?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid Policy 10A, the **treatment plan (plan of care)** for outpatient specialized therapy services must include all of the following:

- **Start and end date** of the therapy treatment plan, with a duration of **no more than six months**
- **Discipline-specific treatment diagnosis** and any related medical diagnoses
- The beneficiary’s **rehabilitative or habilitative potential**
- **Defined goals** for each therapeutic discipline that are:
  - **specific and measurable**, and
  - reasonably expected to be achieved within the duration of the plan
- The **skilled interventions, methodology, procedures, and specific programs** to be used
- **Frequency of services**
- **Length of each treatment visit in minutes**
- **Name, credentials, and signature** of the professional completing the treatment plan, **dated on or before the plan’s start date**  
  [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 3.2.1.6 (effective Feb. 1, 2025; current per amendment check)

Related documentation rule: the provider’s records must include **a copy of the treatment plan**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 7.2 (effective Feb. 1, 2025; current per amendment check)

One additional coverage-related limit in Policy 10A is that therapy is **not covered if it is solely for maintenance**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 4.2.1 (effective Feb. 1, 2025; current per amendment check)

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—HCWD does **not** have a maximum **earned** income limit in the policy text I verified. The policy says HCWD “covers individuals regardless of total countable income,” and it “remove[s] limits on countable income except for the **150% FPL cap on unearned income**,” with sliding-scale premiums instead. [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)] [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

## What income rule applies

To qualify for HCWD, a person must “meet the income requirements for his coverage group.” The income section then states:

- People with **unearned income greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible** for HCWD.
- There is not a surfaced rule imposing a maximum **earned** income cap; instead, higher countable income leads to fees and premiums. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)] [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

## Premiums and fees

The verified HCWD policy says:

- If **total countable income is at or below 150% FPL**: **no cost sharing** other than applicable copayments. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]
- If **total countable income is greater than 150% FPL**: the person must pay a **$50 annual enrollment fee**. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]
- If **total countable monthly income exceeds 200% FPL**: the person must also pay a **monthly premium** in addition to the enrollment fee. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
The federal authority for North Carolina’s CAP/DA waiver is **section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, implemented through the **HCBS waiver rules in 42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**. NC’s own CAP/DA policy says exactly that section 1915(c) authorizes HHS to waive certain Medicaid requirements so the state may offer HCBS to state-specified target groups who meet a **nursing facility level of care**. It also identifies the waiver assurances the state must meet. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective 2025-09-01; no amendments retrieved). [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) (current; no amendments retrieved).

## Federal rule

Under **42 CFR 441.301**, a state’s request for a 1915(c) waiver must include:

- the **assurances** required by **42 CFR 441.302** and the **supporting documentation** required by **42 CFR 441.303**;
- any requested waivers of Medicaid requirements such as **statewideness** and **comparability**, when applicable;
- a statement about whether the state will refuse HCBS when waiver costs would exceed the cost of equivalent institutional care;
- a description of:
  - who will be served,
  - the services to be furnished,
  - qualifications of those developing the plan of care,
  - documentation of individual evaluations, and
  - that services are only for people who, absent waiver services, would require the covered institutional level of care. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## What the state must demonstrate in the waiver application

For a 1915(c) waiver application, the state must demonstrate at least the following:

### 1. Satisfactory waiver assurances
Under **42 CFR 441.302**, CMS will not grant the waiver unless the state gives satisfactory assurances, including:
- **health and welfare** safeguards,
- **financial accountability**, and
- other required assurances reflected in the waiver program structure. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

NC’s CAP/DA policy mirrors this by listing these assurances:
- **Level of Care (LOC)**
- **Administrative Authority**
- **Qualified Providers**
- **Services Plan**
- **Health and Welfare**
- **Financial Accountability**  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 2. Level-of-care criteria and reevaluation
The state must show how it will evaluate and reevaluate beneficiaries to confirm that they would otherwise require institutional care. Federal supporting documentation must include:
- who performs the evaluations,
- the evaluation form used,
- written documentation procedures, and
- regular reevaluation procedures. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

NC’s CAP/DA policy reflects this by requiring that:
- applicants with a reasonable indication of need receive an **individual LOC evaluation**;
- enrolled beneficiaries’ LOC is **reevaluated at least annually** or as specified in the approved waiver; and
- the processes and instruments in the **approved waiver** are used for LOC determination.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 3. Choice between institutional and waiver services
The state must explain how it informs eligible beneficiaries of feasible alternatives and allows them to choose either:
- institutional services, or
- home and community-based waiver services.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

NC’s CAP/DA policy similarly says a beneficiary must **exercise freedom of choice** by choosing to enter or remain in the waiver when otherwise eligible. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 4. Cost neutrality / expenditure limits
The state must support its estimate that the waiver is **cost-neutral**: the average per-capita cost of HCBS plus other Medicaid services under the waiver must **not exceed** the average per-capita cost of services that would have been provided without the waiver. **42 CFR 441.303(f)** sets out that formula. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 5. Target group, services, and waiver size
The state must identify:
- the **target group(s)** it will serve,
- the **services** offered, separately defined,
- and the number of **unduplicated beneficiaries** it intends to serve each year.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## NC implementation context

NC’s CAP/DA policy states that the waiver:
- serves a **state-specified target group**,
- applies to people who meet a **nursing facility level of care**,
- offers services **not otherwise available under the State Plan**, and
- is limited to beneficiaries who are enrolled in Medicaid Direct, meet waiver eligibility criteria, are assigned a CAP/DA slot, and can have health, safety, and well-being maintained in the community with formal and informal supports.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## One important correction to the framing

The key federal authority for this question is **not 42 CFR 431.408**. That section governs the **state public notice process for demonstration projects**. For CAP/DA waiver authority and what must be shown in the application, the controlling federal provisions I could verify are in **42 CFR Part 441, especially §§ 441.301, 441.302, and 441.303**, together with NC’s CAP/DA policy.

If you want, I can also give you a **short attorney-ready citation paragraph** answering this in one block quote style.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** from a nursing facility bed, with **no more than 15 consecutive therapeutic leave days unless NC Medicaid approves more**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective 2024-08-07]

## Conditions that must be met

Therapeutic leave must meet these policy requirements:

- It must be **for therapeutic purposes only**.
- It must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**.
- The **need for the leave must be documented in the resident’s plan of care**.
- The **therapeutic justification for each instance** of leave must be entered in the **resident’s health record**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Additional rules

- The facility must **hold the resident’s bed** during the therapeutic leave.
- The facility may receive **only the Medicaid reimbursement for that bed** during the absence.
- The facility is paid its **full current Medicaid bed rate** for a bed reserved because of therapeutic leave.
- The facility is **not reimbursed** for therapeutic leave days that **exceed the legal limit**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## When therapeutic leave does not apply

Therapeutic leave entitlement **does not apply** when the resident is absent **to receive inpatient or nursing services paid for by Medicaid**, either:

- **elsewhere**, or
- **at a different level of care in the same facility**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Recordkeeping / review

- The therapeutic justification is **subject to review by the State or its agent**.
- Facilities must keep a **cumulative record** of each resident’s therapeutic leave days.
- Residents on therapeutic leave must be identified as such on the facility’s **midnight census**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A Private Duty Nursing provider that terminates services must notify **NC Medicaid**, and the exact required notice depends on whether the beneficiary is **21 and older** or **under 21**.

## Beneficiary age 21 and older
If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary, the provider must **submit the DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form) to NC Medicaid within 5 business days**. If the discharge is because another source of nursing coverage is available, the provider must **notify NC Medicaid and submit the DMA-3513 within 5 business days**, and the notice must include:

- the **last date PDN services were provided and billable to Medicaid**, and
- the **name of the other source of coverage**.

If the **attending physician** discharges the beneficiary, the PDN provider must send NC Medicaid, within **5 business days**:

- the **attending physician’s order to terminate PDN services**, and
- the **DMA-3513**.

If services end because the beneficiary **loses Medicaid eligibility**, or if **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason including hospitalization, the **prior approval process must be started again**. If NC Medicaid terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, **NC Medicaid (or its designee)** must send the beneficiary or legal representative **written adverse notice including appeal rights**.  
Citations: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1. The amendments check returned 3G-1 as the authoritative current document.

## Beneficiary under 21
If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary, the provider must **send a copy of the physician’s order terminating services to NC Medicaid within 5 business days**.

If discharge is because there is **another source of nursing care coverage**, the provider must **notify NC Medicaid in writing**. That notice must state:

- the **last date PDN services were provided and billable to Medicaid**, and
- the **name of the other source of coverage**, as applicable.

If the **attending physician** discharges the beneficiary, the provider must provide NC Medicaid, within **5 business days**, the **physician’s order to terminate beneficiary services**.

If services terminate because of **loss of Medicaid** or because **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** (for example, hospitalization), prior approval must be started again. The policy also specifically says PDN service providers must **notify NC Medicaid when a beneficiary is hospitalized**.  
Citations: [3G-2 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Under 21 Years of Age](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-2-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-under-21-years-age/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1 (effective 2024-05-15). The amendments check returned 3G-2 as the authoritative current document.

## Bottom line
For a PDN termination, the provider’s required notice is primarily to **NC Medicaid**, generally **within 5 business days**, with required discharge documentation. The specific document differs by age group:

- **Age 21 and older:** generally **DMA-3513**, and sometimes also the physician termination order.
- **Under 21:** generally the **physician’s termination order**; for alternate coverage, written notice to NC Medicaid with the required details.

If you want, I can also pull these into a **side-by-side chart for under 21 vs. 21+** or help assess whether the provider also owes the **beneficiary** a separate notice under another authority.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and plan-of-care rules. Those services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis
- **Home health aide services**
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances**
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology/audiology services** as an optional home health benefit  
  ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70)

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided **“at [the beneficiary’s] place of residence.”**  
But the regulation also makes clear that this is **not limited to a private home**. A beneficiary may receive home health services in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** with important exclusions. Home health services **cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**. ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1))

## Excluded settings

For Medicaid home health services, a beneficiary’s “place of residence” **does not include**:

- a **hospital**
- a **nursing facility**
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**

There is a narrow exception for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide. ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c))

The rule also says home health services may not be provided in **any setting in which Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**. ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1))

## Core federal conditions

Federal law also requires that home health services be furnished:

- on **written orders** by a **physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant**, working in accordance with state law, for services covered by § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4);
- as part of a **written plan of care**; and
- with that plan reviewed by the ordering practitioner **every 60 days** for those services.  
  ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a)(2))

For **medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** under § 440.70(b)(3), the services/items must be furnished under the beneficiary’s physician’s orders or orders of another licensed practitioner of the healing arts acting within state-law scope of practice, as part of a written plan of care, with review rules specified in that subsection. ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a)(3), (b)(3))

## Bottom line

Federally, Medicaid **home health services** are defined in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70** as certain nursing, aide, equipment/supplies, and therapy services furnished under required orders and a written plan of care. They must be provided **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**, meaning broadly a setting where **normal life activities take place**, **not** a hospital, nursing facility, or generally an ICF/IID. ([42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70)

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice purposes, **“terminally ill” means the beneficiary has a life expectancy of six months or less**, as reflected in the hospice certification and recertification requirements. The policy text I could verify states that later certification narratives must explain why the clinical findings support **“a life expectancy of six months or less.”** It also requires documentation of the **terminal diagnosis** and current clinical information supporting the diagnoses. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective 2024-03-15), section D, “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness”; [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.3.

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within **two calendar days after a benefit period begins**, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two days, and the written certification must still be obtained before billing. Certifications may be completed no more than **15 calendar days before** the effective date of election, and recertifications no more than **15 calendar days before** the next benefit period. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1.

## Who must sign it

For the **initial 90-day period**, the hospice must obtain a written certification from:

- the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
- the beneficiary’s **attending physician**, if the beneficiary has one.

For **subsequent benefit periods**, only the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice IDG** must certify. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

## What the certification must contain

The certification or recertification must include:

- a physician narrative that **briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis**;
- the physician’s attestation that he or she composed the narrative after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- the **election period dates** to which the certification applies; and
- the certifying physician’s **signature and date**.

For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the findings from the required face-to-face encounter support **a life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), section D, “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

## Face-to-face recertification requirement

A hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner must have a **face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary **before, but no more than 30 calendar days before, the 3rd benefit-period recertification and every recertification after that**, to gather clinical findings for continued hospice eligibility. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1.

per_question.question: What ambulance services are NOT covered by NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not** cover certain ambulance services when either the general coverage rules are not met or the service falls into specific ambulance exclusions.

## General non-covered situations
Ambulance services are not covered if:

- the beneficiary does not meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does not meet the coverage criteria in Section 3.0;

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Speech therapy can be provided by telehealth under NC Medicaid only for a **select set of speech/language evaluation and treatment services**, and only when telehealth is **medically necessary** and used under specific limits. Under current **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A** (effective **Feb. 1, 2025**), telehealth may be used when the beneficiary’s condition makes exposure to others inadvisable, or when the beneficiary is in a remote or underserved location with limited access to qualified providers. It also must generally be **adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement**, unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable. Telehealth must be in the **beneficiary’s best interest**, **not for therapist convenience**, and **never solely to increase therapist productivity**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

## Telehealth conditions for speech therapy

NC Medicaid’s telehealth rule for speech/language services says:

- only a **select set** of speech and language **evaluation and treatment interventions** may be delivered by telehealth;
- telehealth may be medically necessary when:
  - the beneficiary’s medical condition means **exposure to others should be avoided**, or
  - the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved area** with limited access to appropriately qualified providers;
- **unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable**, telehealth must be an **adjunct to in-person care**, not a replacement;
- telehealth must be used in the **best interest of the beneficiary**;
- telehealth may **not** be used as a **convenience for the therapist**; and
- telehealth may **never** be used **solely to increase therapist productivity**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Telehealth eligibility does **not** remove the underlying speech-therapy coverage rules. per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care organizations do **not automatically have to meet a federally mandated minimum MLR in every state**. What federal law requires is that states make each MCO/PIHP/PAHP **calculate and report** its MLR. If a state **chooses** to impose a minimum MLR, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. North Carolina’s implementation evidence I could verify here is that NC has adopted the related **reporting/remittance framework** in its managed care state-plan materials, including repayment of the federal share if remittances are owed. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438); [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

## Federal rule

### 1) What is the federal MLR standard?
Under **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**:

- The state must ensure through its contracts that each **MCO, PIHP, and PAHP calculates and reports an MLR**.  
- **If a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**.  
- So the federal rule is best understood as:
  - **Mandatory calculation and reporting** in all states; and
  - **An optional state-imposed minimum threshold**, which, if used, cannot be below **85%**.  
  [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 2) How is the federal MLR calculated?
Section 438.8 defines the MLR as:

- **Numerator ÷ Denominator**, with possible **credibility adjustment** for partially credible plans.  
- The **numerator** includes, at a high level:
  - incurred claims,
  - expenditures for activities that improve health care quality, and
  - fraud prevention activities.  
- The regulation also specifies adjustments to claims, including items that must be included, deducted, or excluded. For example, the retrieved text shows deductions for:
  - overpayment recoveries from network providers, and
  - prescription drug rebates received and accrued.  
  [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 3) Oversight and remittances
Under **42 C.F.R. § 438.74**:

- The state must annually submit to CMS a summary of each plan’s MLR report.
- That summary must include at least:
  - the numerator,
  - the denominator,
  - the MLR percentage achieved,
  - member months, and
  - any remittances owed.  
- If the state requires remittances when a plan fails to meet the state’s minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the **federal share** of that remittance and submit a separate methodology report.  
  [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina implementation

Based on the NC source I could verify, North Carolina implements the federal MLR framework by assuring that:

- its rates are designed to reasonably achieve a medical loss ratio; and
- **if a remittance is owed** by an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP, the state will:
  - reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance, and
  - submit a separate report describing the methodology used to determine the state and federal shares, along with the annual report summarizing the MCO/PIHP/PAHP reports.  
  [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** plans must **calculate and report** MLR; a state may impose a minimum, but if it does, the minimum must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **North Carolina:** the NC implementation material I verified reflects the federal **reporting/remittance** structure and the obligation to return the **federal share** of remittances to CMS when remittances are required. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

## Currency / amendment status

I checked amendment status for both sources cited here:

- **42 CFR Part 438** — treated as the current authoritative document in the corpus; the retrieved section for **§ 438.74** notes it was **amended at 89 Fed. Reg. 41276 (May 10, 2024)**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under NC Medicaid, **CAR-T cell therapy is covered only when all of the policy’s specific coverage criteria are met**:

- **The CAR-T therapy must be approved by the U.S. FDA**.
- **It must be administered according to the FDA-approved guidelines**, including:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions.
- **It must be administered at a certified or authorized treatment center**.
- **If the product is subject to an FDA-required REMS program**, the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS program, and providers must be trained to manage **cytokine release syndrome (CRS)** and **neurologic toxicities**. [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.2.1, effective 4/1/2025]

NC Medicaid also applies its **general coverage standards**, meaning the service must be:
- individualized and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis,
- safely furnishable, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide, and
- not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider. [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1, effective 4/1/2025]

## Situations the policy says are not covered
CAR-T therapy is **not covered** if, among other things:
- the therapy is **not FDA-approved**,
- it is used **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths,
- a therapy that requires REMS is given at a facility **not enrolled in that REMS program**,
- it is **repeat treatment** after the beneficiary already received another CAR-T therapy,
- psychosocial history limits the beneficiary’s ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care, or
- current beneficiary/caretaker non-compliance makes adherence to the medical regimen improbable. [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.2.1, effective 4/1/2025]

## Prior approval documentation
For prior approval, the policy requires documentation including:
- a physician-signed **letter of medical necessity**,
- verification that the administering facility is a **qualified/authorized treatment center**,
- recent **HIV and hepatitis serologies**,
- diagnostic and procedure results including **bone marrow biopsy** (within policy timelines),
- any other requested diagnostic tests, and
- a **complete psychological and social evaluation**, including compliance history, support network, post-treatment care plan, and mental health/substance use/legal history. [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2, effective 4/1/2025]

## Bottom line
**NC Medicaid covers CAR-T only for FDA-approved use, delivered according to FDA labeling/guidelines, at an appropriately certified/authorized center, with REMS participation and provider training when REMS applies, and only when the beneficiary also meets the policy’s general medical-necessity and coverage requirements.** The current authoritative policy I reviewed is **Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, effective April 1, 2025**, and I found no separate change notice superseding it.

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than their individual base budget, and the base budget is **not** a binding cap on what can be requested or authorized.

## What the policy says

Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P states that a beneficiary **“may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget.”** It also says that the SIS results and base budget are **“guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized,”** and that if the LME/MCO determines the services are **medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget.** [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective Nov. 1, 2016; current authoritative document per amendment check).

## If the participant believes the budget is insufficient

If the person believes their needs cannot be met within the base budget, the policy indicates they can:

- **Request services above the base budget**;
- Seek authorization based on **medical necessity** rather than the budget guideline; and
